note: Curriculum-review artifact, not finished lesson prose. Sequenced pedagogically, not alphabetically. Every learning point traces to at least one evidence-requirement claim in EVIDENCE-RESULTS.json. This inventory is proposed only -- no learning point here is Product-Architect-approved, and none has been used to generate a lesson, storyboard, or assessment.
crossDomainPrerequisiteNote: Cross-domain prerequisites reference the accepted, frozen Batch 01 foundational-mathematics inventory (FM-LP-01 through FM-LP-25, reports/unit202-production-acquisition/batch-01-foundational-mathematics/FOUNDATIONAL-MATHEMATICS-LEARNING-POINTS.json). No FM-LP-* ID is edited, renumbered, or duplicated here; only genuine prerequisites are recorded, not every mathematically-adjacent ID.

learningPoints.title: Basic electron theory
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to describe the basic structure of an atom (nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounding electrons) and explain that a material conducts electricity when its outer electrons are free to move.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: An atom has a tiny nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons equal in number to the protons, making it electrically neutral. In some materials, outer electrons are loosely bound and free to move through the material; this electron mobility is the physical basis of electrical conduction.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Matches Unit 202's Level 2 depth: atomic structure and electron mobility as the qualitative basis for conduction, not quantum/band theory.
explicitExclusions: Electron shells/orbitals and quantum energy levels
applicationTypes: Explain, in outline, why a copper wire conducts electricity but a plastic sheath does not.

learningPoints.title: Current as the rate of flow of electric charge
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge and use the relationship between current, charge and time.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge past a point in a circuit (I = charge/time); the ampere, its SI unit, is one coulomb per second (1 A = 1 C/s).
learningPoints.depthJustification: Calibrated deliberately to teach current AS charge flow (the correct definition) with electron motion as the physical carrier in a conductor, not as an equivalent restatement -- this is the exact false-green risk the acquisition brief for this batch flagged, and this outcome is worded to avoid it.
applicationTypes: Calculate the charge that has flowed in a given time for a stated steady current.

learningPoints.title: Conventional current versus electron flow
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to distinguish conventional current direction (positive to negative) from the actual electron-flow direction (negative to positive) in a DC circuit, and state that both give identical results for circuit calculations.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Conventional current is defined, by a historical convention that predates the discovery of the electron, as flowing from the higher-potential (positive) terminal to the lower-potential (negative) terminal. In a metallic conductor the actual charge carriers are electrons, which physically drift in the opposite direction. Both descriptions are self-consistent and give identical circuit-analysis results.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-HP-ELECUR: conventional current vs electron flow
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept as its own learning point (not merged into EFS-LP-02) so a learner who understands current-as-charge-flow but still confuses the two directional conventions can be diagnosed separately -- a genuinely common, independent misconception at this level.
explicitExclusions: Historical/Franklin biographical detail beyond the reason for the convention
applicationTypes: Label the conventional-current and electron-flow arrows on a simple battery-and-resistor circuit diagram.

learningPoints.title: Conductors and insulators
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain the difference between a conductor and an insulator in terms of resistivity and electron mobility, and give an example of each.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A conductor (e.g. copper) has loosely bound outer electrons free to move, giving very low resistivity and allowing current to flow freely. An insulator (e.g. glass) has tightly bound electrons (essentially zero free electron flow), giving very high resistivity and preventing current flow.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Conductors and insulators are combined into one learning point because they are two poles of the same single comparison, always taught and assessed together at this level -- separating them would create an artificial fragment, not a genuinely independent diagnosis.
applicationTypes: Classify a list of everyday materials (copper, rubber, glass, aluminium, PVC) as conductors or insulators and justify each.

learningPoints.title: Resistance
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state the definition of electrical resistance and its unit.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Resistance is the ratio of the voltage applied across a component to the current that flows through it (R = V/I), measured in ohms (Ω).
learningPoints.depthJustification: Definitional depth only; calculation practice is covered once Ohm's law itself is taught (EFS-LP-07).
applicationTypes: State the unit of electrical resistance and what its ratio compares.

learningPoints.title: Resistivity, its symbol/unit, and R = ρL/A
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain how resistivity differs from resistance, state its symbol (ρ) and unit (ohm-metre), and use R = ρL/A to relate a conductor's resistance to its resistivity, length and cross-sectional area.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Resistivity (symbol ρ, unit ohm-metre, Ω·m) is a property of a material itself, independent of a particular conductor's shape; resistance depends on both the material's resistivity and the conductor's geometry via R = ρL/A, where R = resistance (ohms), ρ = resistivity (Ω·m), L = length (m), A = cross-sectional area (m²). Resistance increases with length and resistivity and decreases with cross-sectional area.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Resistivity's meaning, its symbol, its unit, and the formula connecting it to resistance are combined into one learning point because they are facets of a single teachable idea at this level -- a learner cannot meaningfully be said to understand resistivity without also knowing its symbol/unit and how it relates to R, L and A; separating them would fragment one concept into unassessable slivers. Kept separate from EFS-LP-05 (resistance) because a learner can readily understand resistance (a component's V/I ratio) while not yet grasping that resistivity is a shape-independent material constant -- a genuinely distinct, commonly-confused idea. Rearranging R=rho*L/A for rho, L or A is treated as an application of the general formula-transposition skill (FM-LP-16), not a separate physics fact requiring its own citation -- disclosed in EVIDENCE-RESULTS.json's own scopeNote for this requirement.
applicationTypes: Given a cable's resistivity, length and cross-sectional area, calculate its resistance.
Explain why doubling a conductor's cross-sectional area halves its resistance.

learningPoints.title: Ohm's law (V = IR and its rearrangements)
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state Ohm's law as a conditional relationship for ohmic conductors and use V=IR and its rearrangements (I=V/R, R=V/I) to calculate an unknown voltage, current or resistance.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: For an ohmic conductor, current is directly proportional to the voltage applied across it (resistance is constant over a wide range of voltages); V = IR relates voltage V (volts), current I (amperes) and resistance R (ohms), and rearranges to I = V/R and R = V/I. Ohm's law is a property of ohmic materials, not a universal law true for every component.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-HP-OHMLAW: Ohm's law and V=IR rearrangements
learningPoints.depthJustification: The conceptual relationship (Ohm's law) and its formula/rearrangements are combined into one learning point because they are the same single relationship viewed from two angles -- a learner who 'knows Ohm's law' and one who 'can use V=IR and its rearrangements' are exhibiting the same skill, and splitting them would be an artificial fragment. Deliberately worded as a conditional (ohmic-material) relationship, not an unrestricted universal law, per the depth guidance for this batch.
explicitExclusions: Non-ohmic devices (diodes, thermistors, filament lamps at varying temperature)
applicationTypes: Calculate the current through a known resistor given the supply voltage.
Rearrange V=IR to find the resistance of a component from measured voltage and current.

learningPoints.title: Voltage drop (concept and Vdrop = IR)
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain what a voltage drop is and state that the voltage drop across a resistance carrying current I is Vdrop = IR.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A voltage drop is the potential difference (loss of voltage) that appears across a resistance as a result of current flowing through it; the voltage drop across a resistance R carrying current I is Vdrop = IR -- the same relationship as Ohm's law, applied to describe the voltage lost across that specific resistance.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-UTAH-OHMSLAW: voltage drop across a resistor, V=IR
learningPoints.depthJustification: Definition and formula combined for the same reason as Ohm's law (EFS-LP-07): they are one concept, not two. Kept separate from EFS-LP-09 (the calculation procedure) because understanding what a voltage drop IS and being able to CALCULATE one in a real cable/circuit scenario are genuinely different, independently-diagnosable skills -- exactly the distinction the acquisition brief calls out for this topic.
explicitExclusions: AC voltage drop with reactance/power factor
applicationTypes: State the voltage drop across a 5 ohm resistor carrying 2 A.

learningPoints.title: Calculating voltage drop in a circuit or cable run
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to calculate the voltage drop in a cable run given its tabulated voltage-drop factor, the design current and the cable length, and check the result against a permitted maximum.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A cable's voltage drop is calculated as (tabulated mV/A/m factor) x (design current) x (circuit length) / 1000, giving the drop in volts; the result is checked against a permitted maximum (5% of supply voltage for other-than-lighting circuits, under UK wiring regulations).
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-IET-VDROP: voltage-drop calculation procedure and 5% limit
learningPoints.depthJustification: Scoped to the calculation procedure and its permitted-maximum check, appropriate for Unit 202 foundational depth; does not extend into full cable-selection compliance (correction factors, overcurrent-device coordination), which belongs to a later, more advanced stage of electrical installation study.
explicitExclusions: Correction factors (Ca, Cg, Ci, Cc) for cable current rating
applicationTypes: Calculate the voltage drop for a given cable's mV/A/m rating, a stated load current, and a stated cable run length, and state whether it is within the permitted limit.

learningPoints.title: Series circuit: current
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that the current is the same at every point in a series circuit.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: In a series circuit, the same current flows through every component, because there is only one path for charge to follow: I = I1 = I2 = ...
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept as its own learning point (mirroring the frozen plan's own separation of series current/resistance/voltage into three distinct requirements) because current, resistance and voltage behaviour in a series circuit are three separately-diagnosable relationships -- a learner may master one while still misapplying another, which is exactly the false-green risk this batch's brief names for series/parallel relationships.
applicationTypes: State the current through the second of three lamps wired in series, given the current through the first.

learningPoints.title: Series circuit: resistance
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to calculate the total (equivalent) resistance of resistors connected in series.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: The equivalent resistance of resistors connected in series is the sum of their individual resistances: Req = R1 + R2 + ... + RN.
learningPoints.depthJustification: See EFS-LP-10 for the rationale for keeping series current/resistance/voltage as separate learning points.
explicitExclusions: Series-parallel network reduction (covered once both series and parallel rules are taught)
applicationTypes: Calculate the total resistance of three named resistors connected in series.

learningPoints.title: Series circuit: voltage sharing
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that the supply voltage in a series circuit is shared among the resistors in proportion to their resistance, and that the individual voltage drops sum to the supply voltage.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: In a series circuit, the supply voltage is divided among the resistors in proportion to their resistance, and the sum of the individual voltage drops equals the total supply voltage: deltaV = deltaV1 + deltaV2 + ..., where each deltaVi = I*Ri (the same current I flows through each).
learningPoints.depthJustification: See EFS-LP-10 for the rationale for keeping series current/resistance/voltage as separate learning points; voltage sharing is proportional reasoning applied to resistance ratios, hence the FM-LP-10 (direct proportion) cross-domain prerequisite.
explicitExclusions: Voltage-divider circuits with a loaded output (a separate, more advanced application)
applicationTypes: Given three series resistors and a supply voltage, calculate the voltage drop across each.

learningPoints.title: Parallel circuit: voltage
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that the voltage is the same across every branch of a parallel circuit.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: In a parallel circuit, the voltage (potential difference) across every branch is the same and equal to the supply voltage: deltaV = deltaV1 = deltaV2 = ...
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept separate from parallel current/resistance for the same reason series current/resistance/voltage are kept separate (see EFS-LP-10) -- each is independently diagnosable and a frequent, distinct source of learner confusion.
explicitExclusions: Non-ideal (loaded) sources with internal resistance affecting branch voltages
applicationTypes: State the voltage across the second of three lamps wired in parallel, given the supply voltage.

learningPoints.title: Parallel circuit: current
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that current divides among the branches of a parallel circuit and that the branch currents sum to the total current.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: In a parallel circuit, the total current divides among the branches, and the individual branch currents sum to the total current entering (and leaving) the parallel combination: I = I1 + I2 + ...
learningPoints.depthJustification: See EFS-LP-13/EFS-LP-10.
explicitExclusions: Kirchhoff's current law for general (non-simple-parallel) networks
applicationTypes: Given the current through two of three parallel branches and the total supply current, find the current through the third branch.

learningPoints.title: Parallel circuit: equivalent resistance
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to calculate the equivalent resistance of resistors connected in parallel, and explain why it is always less than the smallest individual resistor.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: The equivalent (total) resistance of resistors in parallel is found from 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... + 1/RN; the equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest individual resistor in the combination.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Combining reciprocal resistances requires fraction arithmetic (adding fractions with unlike denominators, then taking a reciprocal) -- exactly the skill Batch 01's own inventory flagged as a foundational prerequisite for 'parallel-resistance-style formulae' (see FOUNDATIONAL-MATHEMATICS-LEARNING-POINTS.json's foundationalPrerequisitesForElectricalCalculations list), so FM-LP-01/FM-LP-02 are recorded here as the genuine cross-domain prerequisite that batch anticipated.
explicitExclusions: The product-over-sum shortcut for exactly two resistors (a calculation convenience, not separately assessed knowledge)
applicationTypes: Calculate the equivalent resistance of two or three named resistors connected in parallel.

learningPoints.title: Electrical power formulas (P=VI, P=I²R, P=V²/R)
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state the three equivalent forms of the electrical power formula and select the appropriate one for the quantities known in a given calculation.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Electrical power is the product of voltage and current, P = VI. Using Ohm's law (V=IR), this is equivalent to P = I^2R (used when current and resistance are known) and to P = V^2/R (used when voltage and resistance are known, and, in a source-and-load circuit, only where the source's own internal resistance can be treated as negligible compared with the load).
learningPoints.depthJustification: The three power forms are combined into one learning point because they are algebraically equivalent expressions of a single relationship, and the frozen requirement plan itself frames 'the conditions under which P=VI, P=I^2R and P=V^2/R are used' as one combined concern -- unlike series/parallel relationships, these are not separately-taught facts but one relationship viewed three ways. The P=V^2/R form's 'where appropriate' condition (negligible source/internal resistance) is stated explicitly, not glossed over, per the depth guidance for this batch.
explicitExclusions: AC power with power factor/reactive power
Energy (kWh) calculations from power and time (a distinct, not-yet-acquired Unit 202 topic)
applicationTypes: Given a resistor's current and resistance, calculate the power dissipated using the most appropriate formula.
Explain which power formula to use when only voltage and resistance are known.

learningPoints.title: Calculating power in a DC circuit
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to carry out a DC-circuit power calculation: reduce a network of series and parallel resistors to a single equivalent resistance, then apply the appropriate power formula.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A suitable procedure for a DC-circuit power calculation is: (1) reduce the circuit's series and parallel resistor combinations step by step to a single equivalent resistance; (2) apply the appropriate power relationship (P=VI, P=I^2R or P=V^2/R, as the known quantities allow) to find the required unknown.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-ETSU-PHYS2020: worked multi-resistor DC power-calculation example
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept separate from EFS-LP-16 (the power-formula concept) because carrying out a full multi-step DC circuit calculation (network reduction, then formula selection and application) is a distinct, more demanding procedural skill from knowing the formulas themselves -- a learner may know all three formulas but not yet be able to apply them within a multi-resistor network.
explicitExclusions: Multi-loop networks requiring Kirchhoff's rules (not reducible to simple series/parallel combination)
applicationTypes: Given a network of series and parallel resistors and a supply voltage, calculate the total power delivered by the source.

learningPoints.title: Thermal effect of current (Joule heating)
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that current flowing through a resistance generates heat, and that the rate of heat generation is proportional to the square of the current.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: The thermal effect of current (Joule heating) is the conversion of electrical energy into heat as current flows through a resistance; the rate of heat production is P=I^2R=IV, so it increases with the square of the current.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept separate from EFS-LP-19 (fuse operation) because understanding the general thermal effect (heat generation proportional to I^2R) and understanding how a specific protective device exploits it are different, independently-diagnosable outcomes -- a learner can know Joule heating in the abstract without yet connecting it to how a fuse actually works.
applicationTypes: Explain why doubling the current through a fixed resistor quadruples the rate of heat generated.

learningPoints.title: Fuse operation as an application of the thermal effect
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain how a fuse uses the thermal effect of current to protect a circuit from excessive current.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A fuse contains a thin conductor that melts at a designed (low) temperature; when the circuit current becomes high enough to generate sufficient heat to reach that melting point, the conductor melts and breaks the circuit -- a direct practical application of the thermal effect as a protective mechanism.
learningPoints.depthJustification: This underlying evidence requirement carries OPTIONAL_CONTEXT (lower) acquisition priority in the frozen plan, reflecting its status as a practical illustration rather than a core examinable fact; it is nonetheless fully evidenced and READY here.
explicitExclusions: Fuse rating selection/coordination with cable current-carrying capacity (a more advanced, not-yet-acquired installation-design topic)
Circuit-breaker/MCB operating mechanisms (a different protective device)
applicationTypes: Explain, in terms of the thermal effect, why a fuse rated for a lower current than the fault current will break the circuit.

learningPoints.title: Chemical effect of current (electrolysis)
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain, in outline, how passing an electric current through an electrolyte causes a chemical reaction, and describe what happens at the anode and cathode.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: The chemical effect of an electric current (electrolysis) is the chemical decomposition of a substance caused by passing a current through it via an electrolyte: oxidation occurs at the positive electrode (anode) and reduction occurs at the negative electrode (cathode), producing new substances -- for example, passing current through water containing an electrolyte decomposes it into hydrogen gas at the cathode and oxygen gas at the anode.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Matches Level 2 depth: qualitative mechanism (electrolyte, anode/cathode roles, oxidation/reduction, decomposition) via a single worked example, not electrochemical cell potentials or Faraday's laws of electrolysis.
explicitExclusions: Faraday's laws of electrolysis (quantitative mass/charge relationships)
Electrode potentials and the electrochemical series
Industrial electrolysis processes (e.g. aluminium extraction) beyond a passing example
applicationTypes: State which gas is produced at the cathode when water containing a suitable electrolyte is electrolysed.
